questions.q: Coverage rose, but there's no automatic checker for this task. What now?
questions.a: Train a verifier to score answers and pick the top one. Lightman et al. found a reward model trained on feedback for every step picked better than one trained only on final answers, and both beat majority voting, when choosing among 1,860 answers per MATH problem.

teach.title: How it works: measure two numbers, then fix the weak one

questions.q: Why not report pass@k as the result?
questions.a: pass@k assumes a perfect checker picks the right sample for you. In deployment you submit one answer, so pass@k is a ceiling on what any selector can reach, not the score you'll get.

questions.q: Why draw 200 samples to estimate pass@10?
questions.a: With many more samples than k, the estimate averages over many possible sets of 10, so it's less noisy. The Codex paper used n = 200 for k up to 100, with a formula that stays unbiased.

teach.title: How it works: measure two numbers, then fix the weak one

questions.q: What's the difference between coverage and the solve rate you actually get?
questions.a: Coverage is the share of problems where at least one sample is right. The solve rate is the share where the answer you hand in is right, which depends on how you pick among the samples.

questions.q: Why can't majority voting take advantage of a rare right answer?
questions.a: The vote hands in the most common answer. If the right answer turns up in 2% of samples and a wrong one in 30%, more samples make the right one appear but never make it the most common.

questions.q: Coverage and solve rate are both flat as samples grow. What do you suspect?
questions.a: The samples are too alike to add new answers, for example because the temperature is at or near 0. Counting distinct final answers per problem shows it.
